set.hook: The Roca brothers' Girona flagship, three MICHELIN stars and forty years old in 2026.
set.why: Joan, Josep and Jordi Roca opened El Celler in 1986 beside their parents' family restaurant in Taialà, on the edge of Girona, and the house turns forty this year. To mark it, Joan Roca presented a menu of forty small dishes at San Sebastián Gastronomika on 5 October 2026, built around the tasting format and using augmented reality at the table. The standing menu, Festival, runs to snacks, twelve dishes and three desserts, and the whole table eats it.
set.verdict: The grand night of the coast, for guests who will plan a trip around one dinner. Book the Festival menu with Josep Roca's wine pairing, and ask whether the fortieth-anniversary menu is being served on your date.

set.hook: Albert Sastregener's two-star kitchen in an old carriage works on the road through Corçà.
set.why: Bo.TiC opened in 2007 and took its second MICHELIN star in the 2021 guide, announced in December 2020 alongside Cinc Sentits and Culler de Pau. set.hook: A roadside masia on the Sant Feliu road, run by the Gascons siblings, starred since 2008.
set.why: Els Tinars began in 1978 as a roadside restaurant that the Gascons parents opened in a centuries-old farmhouse beside the Costa Brava road; their own parents had run the Bahía in Sant Feliu de Guíxols in the 1950s. Marc Gascons now cooks and runs it with his sister Elena, and in July 2025 he won the Premi Nacional de Gastronomia for author cuisine. The most requested dish is a tartare of Palamós prawn whose garnish changes with the season.
set.verdict: For guests who want serious Catalan cooking without a laboratory feel, at a fraction of the two- and three-star bills. Order the Palamós prawn tartare and the seasonal menu.

set.hook: A family house on Plaça de Sant Pere, by the fishing port, where the Palamós red prawn is grilled plainly.
set.why: La Gamba has fed Palamós since the 1960s (the old record says 1967, under the Cuadrat family), a few steps from the quay where the town's red prawn is sold at auction each afternoon. Time Out calls it a family restaurant with very little embellishment in the cooking, and that is the point: the gamba goes on the grill with salt. The other house plates are older Empordà ideas, chicken with lobster and black rice.
set.verdict: For anyone who wants the gamba de Palamós a short walk from where it is landed, without a tasting menu around it. Order the grilled prawns first, then a rice; reviews in April 2026 were split, so judge on the prawn.

set.hook: A few tables in a Roses back street where Rafa Cantero cooks the morning's shellfish on a hot plate.
set.why: Rafa Cantero has run this small room on Carrer de Sant Sebastià for more than three decades; Jancis Robinson wrote in 2013 of thirty years at the planxa, with Rosa serving. set.hook: A family hotel kitchen on the steps above Llafranc bay, seventy years old in 2026.
set.why: Casamar is a family house that the Casellas siblings say turns seventy this year; their grandparents opened it. set.hook: Shared plates from the three chefs behind Disfrutar, in an old stone house on the Cadaqués riverbed.
set.why: Before Disfrutar in Barcelona, Mateu Casañas, Oriol Castro and Eduard Xatruch, who met in the elBulli kitchen at Cala Montjoi over the hill, opened this room in Cadaqués in 2012. The rule is in the name: nothing arrives as an individual plate, everything goes to the middle. The chef's menu now runs to about ten savoury courses and three sweets. set.hook: Watch the Palamós catch sold at the falling-price auction, then cook fish with the quay's own kitchen.
set.why: The Palamós fish market sells its catch by Dutch auction: the price falls on a board until a buyer stops it. The Museu de la Pesca runs half-hour guided visits that explain the bidding live through a large window over the floor, usually at 4.30pm and 5pm; they cost EUR 3.50 in 2025. Next door, the Espai del Peix kitchen teaches what to do with the less famous fish, and cooked at the 11th Fira de la Gamba on 13 June 2026.

set.hook: L'Escala's oldest salting house: anchovies cured on site since 1888, with a museum and a tasting terrace.
set.why: The Solés family has salted anchovies in L'Escala since 1888, and the factory stands in the oldest salting building left in the town. For the company's 130th anniversary it opened a museum inside the working plant, with audio guides in seven languages on how the fish is layered in salt, pressed and filleted by hand. The ticket ends with a tasting on the terrace outside, where the shop sells the jars.
set.verdict: The larder stop for anyone provisioning a galley or taking food home. Do the museum and tasting, then buy the fillets in oil and a jar of seitons.

set.hook: Girona's municipal food hall, opened in November 1944, where the stalls trade from early morning.
set.why: The Mercat del Lleó opened on 3 November 1944, in a building whose architects were chosen by the Franco regime after the Civil War, and it is still the city's main covered food market. Stallholders start early: a 2008 report noted many of them begin winding down well before lunchtime, which is why a Friday-afternoon opening was debated then. Inside are Girona's butchers, fishmongers, cheese and charcuterie counters, and in autumn the wild mushrooms.
set.verdict: Go in the morning, before the counters thin out, and shop for the galley or a picnic: botifarra, Empordà cheese, autumn bolets. Pair it with coffee in the Old Town across the river.

set.hook: The specialty coffee bar a Tour de France rider and his wife opened in 2015, bikes hung on the walls.
set.why: Christian Meier, a Canadian professional cyclist, and his wife Amber opened La Fábrica in March 2015, soon after he had ridden the Tour de France, and at the time it was the only café in Girona roasting its own beans. The beans now come from their second shop, Espresso Mafia, where Christian roasts on a 15-kilo Joper. Old bicycles hang on the stone walls, and riders in kit fill the street terrace each morning.
set.verdict: Coffee first: a flat white or filter, then a cinnamon bun if the queue allows. For crew on a rest day, or anyone curious about Girona's cycling life.

set.hook: Jordi Roca's ice-cream shop, born from the dessert trolley at El Celler de Can Roca.
set.why: Rocambolesc began as the dessert cart at El Celler de Can Roca, which Jordi Roca and Alejandra Rivas wanted to wheel out onto the streets of Girona; the shop opened on Carrer de Santa Clara in 2012. It has since grown a confectionery next door (2022) and the Bikineria, a toasted-sandwich counter on Carrer de les Hortes. Opinionated About Dining placed the gelateria 60th on its Cheap Eats in Europe list for 2025.
set.verdict: The walk-in way to taste the Roca brothers' kitchen. Order the panet, warm ice-cream brioche, or a soft-serve with toppings; queues build on summer evenings.
